concept: Priority fee estimation and compute budget instructions

claims.text: The base fee is a flat 5,000 lamports per required signature. It does not depend on the CUs the transaction requests or uses. The priority fee is charged on top of the base fee. (high confidence)

Wallets and fee-injection code that prepend Compute Budget instructions at index 0 break durable-nonce transactions, because the runtime only recognises a nonce transaction when AdvanceNonceAccount is instruction 0. A Phantom user reported on devnet that the modified transaction 'can never land'; the thread was closed by redirecting to support with no public fix confirmed. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-12)

Query the writable accounts the transaction will lock (pool, vault, user token accounts, oracle), not program IDs. Only writable accounts enter the per-account map, and an empty account list returns only the block-wide minimum. Re-estimate for each transaction from a recent sample, because hot-account fees move within seconds, and apply a hard per-transaction cap. Jupiter likewise advises capping the price and validating it before signing, because estimates can spike when recent blocks hold extreme bids. (medium confidence)

Triton extends getRecentPrioritizationFees with an optional percentile parameter, an integer from 1 to 10,000 (5000 is the median, steps of 0.01%). For each block it returns that percentile of the CU prices paid by non-vote transactions; with account addresses it takes the percentile over the transactions that write-lock each account and returns the highest. Without the parameter it returns the standard minimum. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Standard method for sizing the limit: simulate the transaction with a high placeholder limit, read unitsConsumed, then set SetComputeUnitLimit to that value plus a 10-20% margin. The margin covers state changes between simulation and execution; the simulated figure can be higher or lower than what the landed transaction uses. (high confidence)

Code that reads limits or fees by scanning Compute Budget instructions finds nothing on v1 transactions. Read transactionConfig first and fall back to the instruction scan for legacy and v0. To compare a v0 rate with a v1 total, convert the rate with ceil(price * CU limit / 1,000,000). JSON-RPC readers need maxSupportedTransactionVersion set to the integer 1, or getBlock and getTransaction fail with error -32015 on v1 data. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-15)

Agave's scheduler ranks queued transactions by priority = reward x 1,000,000 / (1 + cost). Reward is the validator's fee income: the priority fee plus the non-burned share of the base fee. Cost is the cost-model total for signatures, write locks, instruction data, program execution (the requested or default CU limit) and loaded-accounts data. Rank therefore depends on lamports per unit of total requested cost, not on the micro-lamport price alone. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Because requested CUs sit in the cost denominator, a tighter CU limit (and a tighter loaded-accounts data limit) raises a transaction's rank at the same total lamport fee, while raising only the price spends more for the same cost. A practitioner post argues that right-sizing the CU limit moves rank more than a higher price does. (medium confidence)

Averages, medians or percentiles of the raw per-slot values are statistics of floors, not of what landed transactions paid. In congestion the distribution above the floor widens where this call cannot see it, so such estimates run low exactly when it matters. The reverse also happens: one overpaying transaction on a quiet account sets that account's value for the whole slot. Triton calls the default value often zero and a poor signal for the competitive fee. (medium confidence)

If the limit is below the CUs the transaction needs, execution stops with InstructionError::ComputationalBudgetExceeded ('Computational budget exceeded') and the fee is still charged. Simulation can understate later usage because state moves between simulation and landing (routes, tick arrays, Token-2022 transfer hooks). A variable-cost swap therefore needs a larger margin than a fixed-cost transfer, and a re-simulation close to submission. (medium confidence)

A CU limit taken from a simulation can be too low at landing time, because account state changes between simulation and execution (swap routes through Token-2022 transfer hooks or changing tick arrays). The result is ComputationalBudgetExceeded and a paid, failed transaction. The sources suggest a 10-15% margin, re-simulating when a program is upgraded or the instruction mix changes, and caching typical CU use per transaction type instead of simulating every send. (medium confidence)

The fee market is per writable account, so estimates should pass the writable state accounts the transaction will lock (pool, token accounts, oracle). Passing a program ID returns near-empty data and a misleading picture; omitting accounts gives a network-wide view that is wrong for contested accounts. (medium confidence)

Estimate the price per account set, not network-wide. Pass the writable accounts the transaction will lock (pool state, vaults, user token accounts) to getRecentPrioritizationFees. Do not pass program IDs: programs are read-only in user transactions, so the per-account fee map holds almost no data for them and the result misleads. (high confidence)

A durable-nonce transaction must carry System AdvanceNonceAccount as instruction 0 (NONCED_TX_MARKER_IX_INDEX = 0, with the nonce account first and writable). Otherwise the runtime does not treat it as a nonce transaction, so the nonce value used as recent_blockhash is not accepted. Add Compute Budget instructions after instruction 0. Solana's Kit example sets the nonce lifetime first, which prepends AdvanceNonceAccount, and adds the other instructions afterwards. (high confidence)
